\section{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}
% 2026-09-21 house shape: four setup blocks, Exp-N paragraphs (pointer -> axis -> headline -> highlight -> anomaly), case studies
% continue the numbering; no subsections; monochrome figures (ours black, STrees grey); short captions.  Numbers: tables/*.tex
% generated by make_tables.py from the records, macros in tables/*_stats.tex; case-study numbers from case/*.json.

\stitle{Hardware.}
% 2026-09-22 compaction: the four setup blocks in fourteen sentences.
All algorithms are implemented in C++ and run single-threaded on a laptop (Apple M-series) and two Ubuntu 22.04 servers, server 1 and server 2 (GCC 11.4, 96 cores, 503~GB of memory each).
%
We never ran two timing runs at once on one machine.
%
Jobs of other users ran on the servers at the same time, with a load average of 1 to 8 on the 96 cores.
%
One core of the laptop is 1.5 to 3 times faster than one core of a server, so laptop and server latencies are not directly comparable, and every table and figure names its machine.

\stitle{Algorithms.}
\chainidx is the index of Sections~\ref{sec:index} to~\ref{sec:construction}, built by \build and queried by \query.
%
\strees is the index of Section~\ref{sec:strees}, one tree and one depth-first array per size with every value stored.
%
Its size is computed from the same core values and trees as \chainidx, and its query latency is measured on the same decomposition and the same queries.
%
\cnd is the published counting-based nucleus decomposition~\cite{Zhang2026NucleusCounting}, run once per size with its default settings.
%
It computes core values only, so it is compared on build time and not on index size.

\stitle{Datasets.}
We use \numgraphs{} real graphs from five families, collaboration, citation, web, product co-purchase, and social and communication networks, with $1{,}005$ to $4{,}049{,}537$ vertices and largest cliques of $7$ to $500$ vertices.
%
Table~\ref{tab:size} lists them with their family and their largest clique size $s_{\max}$, so the sizes with a nonzero value are $2$ to $s_{\max}$.
%
Three larger graphs, \textsf{com-lj}, \textsf{ca-hollywood-2009} and \textsf{com-orkut}, run out of the 503~GB of memory of the servers while the clique tree of the peel is built.

\stitle{Metrics.}
Queries draw a vertex that lies in an edge and a size $s$ between $2$ and its clique number.
%
The workload has $20{,}000$ community queries at the vertex's own level, $k=\core{s}{v}$, $20{,}000$ at half that level (rounded down, at least $1$), $1{,}000$ at $k=1$, and $200{,}000$ value queries.
%
Each workload runs six times, the first as a warm-up, and the latency is the median over the other five of the total time divided by the number of queries.
%
Index sizes are measured in memory, and build times exclude the reading of the graph.

\expsection{Index size}
Table~\ref{tab:size} lists every graph with its number of chains, its vertices per chain and its share of values stored explicitly.
%
The next columns are the sizes of \chainidx and of \strees with their ratio, and the last two the build time and memory usage of \build (Exp-6).
%
\chainidx is \ratiomin$\times$ to \ratiomax$\times$ smaller than \strees, median \ratiomedian$\times$, and the ratio grows with the number of vertices per chain.
%
\emailcore, with $1{,}005$ vertices in $667$ chains, $1.5$ per chain, is the worst case at \ratiomin$\times$, and \webuk, with $129{,}632$ vertices in $839$ chains, $154$ per chain, is the best at \ratiomax$\times$.
%
The two collaboration graphs with the largest cliques, \textsf{ca-coauthors-dblp} and \textsf{dblp-coauthor}, compress by $45.8\times$ and $12.0\times$, the web graphs by $5.7\times$ to $48.7\times$, and the social graphs by $2.9\times$ to $15.9\times$.
%
If the graph keeps its original vertex ids, the index also stores the permutation from ids to labels (Section~\ref{sec:labels}), $n$ labels, which lowers the ratios to \permmin$\times$ to \permmax$\times$ (median \permmedian$\times$).

\expsection{Size by part}
% 2026-09-22 compaction: six sentences.
On the collaboration, web and product graphs the per-size trees with their run arrays are $58$ to $74$ percent of the index.
%
The records of the chains (Section~\ref{sec:values}) are $23$ to $41$ percent.
%
On the social and citation graphs, where chains are shorter, the records reach $44$ to $58$ percent.
%
Only the residues are stored (Theorem~\ref{thm:tail}): the share of the pairs $(v,s)$ with a nonzero value whose value is a residue (Table~\ref{tab:size}) ranges from \storedmin{} to \storedmax{} percent, median \storedmedian{} percent.
%
\webuk has $23.5$ million such pairs and stores one residue in total, \emailcore stores \storedmax{} percent of its values, and on \dblp $84{,}010$ of $1{,}246{,}933$ pairs are residues, $9{,}737$ values once stored per chain.
%
The share is lowest on the graphs with large cliques, where most of a vertex's values lie in its tail.
%
It is highest on the sparse social and citation graphs, where the certification point is close to the clique number.

\expsection{Design study}
% 2026-09-22 compaction: the table of the five layouts is a paragraph with the ranges as macros (tables/layout_stats.tex); the chain factor was misquoted as 4.5 (data: 4.8).
We measured the layout decisions one at a time on \textsf{ca-GrQc}, \textsf{ca-HepPh}, \dblp, \textsf{web-Stanford} and \textsf{amazon0302}.
%
Trees over twin classes (Section~\ref{sec:chains}) do not help, since twin classes have $1.03$ to $1.28$ vertices on average.
%
They are at best \laytwinmax$\times$ smaller than \strees and on three of the five graphs larger.
%
Trees over chains with an explicit vertex-to-chain map are \laychainmin$\times$ to \laychainmax$\times$ smaller than \strees.
%
Aligned labels, which remove the map, bring the factor to \layalignmin$\times$ to \layalignmax$\times$, and the runs with their entries to \layfinalmin$\times$ to \layfinalmax$\times$.
%
We also measured the skyline layout of SGL~\cite{SGL} over chains, one entry per chain and non-dominated size.
%
It took $1.01$ to $1.12$ times the space of the tree layout and $2.3$ to $6.3$ times longer to answer an own-level query, so it is not part of the index.

\expsection{Query latency}
% 2026-09-22 compaction: the per-graph query table is gone; Figure fig:regimes (three panels) carries the levels, the listing ratio against vertices per range, and the locating strips.
Figure~\ref{fig:regimes} reports the community queries of the three levels for both indexes on the \stpairs{} (graph, machine) pairs measured together.
%
Locating takes \locmin{} to \locmax{}~ns at the own level, median \locmedian{}~ns.
%
\strees takes about half, since it reads the own node from the vertex directly.
%
Panel (c) gives the medians per level: \ownmedian{}~ns at the own level, \halfmedian{}~ns at half the level and \rootmedian{}~ns at $k=1$ for \chainidx.
%
With the jump pointers, the climb to the root costs no more than the own-level query, and the half-level climb, which stops at an interior node, costs at most \halfmax{}~ns.
%
The parent-pointer climb of \strees has no such bound and costs up to \stlocdeepmax$\times$ the time of \chainidx: on \textsf{ca-coauthors-dblp}, whose hierarchy has $5{,}543$ levels, $1{,}086$~ns against $109$~ns.
%
Listing time, panel (a), grows linearly with the answer size for both indexes, at $0.05$ to $0.5$~ns per vertex above a fixed cost of a few nanoseconds.
%
\strees lists a community by one memory copy of its slice, and \chainidx reports one range per run however many labels it expands to.
%
Panel (b) plots the ratio of the two listing times against the mean number of vertices per range.
%
\chainidx is faster where the answer is a few long ranges, on the social, product and web graphs.
%
It is slower where the answer is split into short ranges: \emailcore, \textsf{cit-HepPh} and \textsf{ca-AstroPh} have $2$ to $5$ vertices per range.
%
Over the \stpoints{} (graph, level) points the ratio ranges from \stmin{} to \stmax{} (median \stmedian), and \chainidx is the faster one on \stfaster{} of them.
%
Value queries take \valmin{} to \valmax{}~ns, median \valmedian{}~ns.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_regimes.pdf}
\caption{Community queries: (a) listing time by answer size and level, (b) listing time of \strees over that of \chainidx by vertices per range, (c) locating time by level.}\label{fig:regimes}
\end{figure*}

\expsection{Latency by clique size and by answer size}
% 2026-09-22 compaction: eight sentences.
Figure~\ref{fig:profile} separates two variables that the workload above averages, the clique size and the answer size, on two representative graphs measured on server 2, \textsf{web-BerkStan} and \textsf{cit-Patents}.
%
The other graphs show the same trends.
%
Panels (a) and (b) plot the locating and the listing time against the clique size.
%
They use $5{,}000$ own-level queries per size $s$, with the vertex drawn uniformly among the vertices that lie in an $s$-clique.
%
Panel (c) plots the listing time against the answer size.
%
\chainidx locates in \proflocmin{} to \proflocmax{}~ns at every size, highest between $s=3$ and $6$, where the per-size trees have the most nodes, and \strees in \profstlocmin{} to \profstlocmax{}~ns.
%
At $s=2$ and $3$, where the answers are large and consist of a few long runs, \chainidx lists the answer in \profsmallinvmax{} to \profsmallinvmin{} times the time of the memory copy.
%
From $s=4$ on, where the own-level answers shrink and spread over many ranges, the copy is faster, up to \profbigmax$\times$ at $s=\profbigs$ on \textsf{cit-Patents}, where the mean answer has \profbigout{} vertices in \profbigranges{} ranges.
%
Panel (c) sorts the $20{,}000$ own-level queries of the workload above by answer size into ten groups of equal count.
%
Below $10^5$ vertices the copy is \profdeclowmin$\times$ to \profdeclowmax$\times$ faster, between $10^5$ and $10^6$ the gap closes, and from $10^6$ vertices on the two agree within \profdechigh{} percent.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_profile.pdf}
\caption{Own-level latency by clique size and by answer size.}\label{fig:profile}
\end{figure*}

\expsection{Construction}
The last two columns of Table~\ref{tab:size} give the build time of \chainidx, which covers the clique tree, the peel of every size and the index passes of Section~\ref{sec:construction}, and its memory usage.
%
The index passes are a few percent of the time, the clique tree and the peel are the rest, and the memory usage is that of the clique tree.
%
The build takes $0.01$~s on \textsf{ca-GrQc} and $221$~s on \textsf{dblp-coauthor}, the graph of $4$ million vertices, with $8.8$~GB of memory there.
%
\dblp is built in $0.84$~s with $157$~MB.

\expsection{Scalability}
Figure~\ref{fig:scale} follows \textsf{cit-Patents} and \textsf{web-BerkStan} on server 2 through vertex-induced random samples of $20$, $40$, $60$ and $80$ percent of their vertices up to the full graph.
%
The panels show the sizes of both indexes, the build time of \chainidx and of \cnd run once per size, and the own-level locating and listing time of both indexes.
%
A sample of a fraction $p$ of the vertices keeps about $p^2$ of the edges, so the samples grow in size and in density at once.
%
The largest cliques of \textsf{web-BerkStan} go from $45$ to $202$ vertices.
%
\chainidx grows with the vertices, at $2.9$ to $3.2$ bytes per vertex on \textsf{cit-Patents} and $5.3$ to $12.6$ on \textsf{web-BerkStan}, whose cliques grow with the sample, while \strees grows with the number of (vertex, size) pairs.
%
The ratio of the two sizes therefore rises along each curve, from $7.7\times$ to $12.1\times$ on \textsf{cit-Patents} and from $6.4\times$ to $19.2\times$ on \textsf{web-BerkStan}.
%
The build time grows faster than the sample, from $0.56$ to $19.5$ seconds as the vertices of \textsf{cit-Patents} grow five times and from $0.21$ to $65.6$ seconds on \textsf{web-BerkStan}.
%
\cnd once per size grows faster still.
%
Its build and peel time divided by the build time of \chainidx rises from $6.6$ to $18$ along the \textsf{cit-Patents} curve and lies between $61$ and $135$ along the \textsf{web-BerkStan} curve.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_scale.pdf}
\caption{Scalability over vertex-induced samples.}\label{fig:scale}
\end{figure*}

\expsection{Against one decomposition per size}
% 2026-09-22 compaction: the per-pair table is Figure fig:prior (log-log scatter with the 10x/100x/1000x lines).
Figure~\ref{fig:prior} plots, for the \priorgraphs{} (graph, machine) pairs with both records, the build and peel time of \cnd summed over the sizes $2$ to $s_{\max}$ against the one build of \chainidx on the same machine.
%
\chainidx is built faster by \priormin$\times$ on \textsf{com-amazon} (six sizes) to \priormax$\times$ on \webuk{} ($499$ sizes), median \priormedian$\times$.
%
The clique tree is built once instead of once per size, and the peel of one size is reused by the next through the certificate of Theorem~\ref{thm:replay} and the bound of Section~\ref{sec:construction}.
%
The ratio grows with the number of sizes: on \textsf{web-BerkStan} ($201$ sizes) the $2.0$ hours of build and peel of \cnd become $66$ seconds, and on \webuk{} $15.7$ hours become $70$ seconds.
%
One run of \cnd is also the cost of answering a community query without an index, a decomposition at the queried size.
%
That is seconds to minutes per query on these graphs, against the nanoseconds of Figure~\ref{fig:regimes}.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_prior.pdf}
\caption{\cnd once per size against one build of \chainidx.}\label{fig:prior}
\end{figure}

\expsection{Case Study I: the best size per query}
% 2026-09-22 compaction: thirteen sentences.
Three graphs of the SNAP collection~\cite{leskovec2016snap} come with ground-truth communities, of which SNAP provides the $5{,}000$ of highest quality: \dblp (publication venues), \textsf{com-amazon} (product categories) and \textsf{com-youtube} (user groups).
%
For a member $v$ of a ground-truth community $D$ and every size $s\le\omg{v}$ and level $k$, we score the $(s,k)$-core of $v$ by its F1 score against $D$.
%
The F1 score is the harmonic mean of the precision and the recall of the core as a guess of $D$.
%
The whole $(s,k)$ space of a query is scanned from the index without listing a community, in $1$ to $50~\mu$s.
%
The intersection is counted by testing, for every member of $D$, whether its own node lies in the subtree of the core, and the size of the core comes from its entries.
%
Since the scale of $k$ differs between sizes, we compare the best level of each size.
%
The $k$-core at its best level, that is, size $2$, is the first choice.
%
We compare it with the triangle size $s=3$ at its best level, the best single size for the graph at its best level, and the best size and level chosen per query.
%
\sstitle{No single size is right on \dblp.}
The best size spreads over $2$ to $8$.
%
Size $2$ is best for $26$ percent of the queries, size $3$ for $23$ percent, size $4$ for $18$, size $5$ for $13$, and sizes $6$ and above for $20$.
%
Choosing the size and level per query gives an F1 of $0.179$, $3.6\times$ the $0.049$ of the $k$-core and $1.2\times$ the $0.147$ of the best fixed size, $s=5$, at its best level.
%
For $74$ percent of the queries, some size other than $2$ beats the $k$-core at every level.
%
\sstitle{One size can be enough.}
On \textsf{com-amazon} the best size is $3$ for $59$ percent of the queries.
%
The triangle size alone reaches $0.824$ against $0.851$ for the per-query choice, $1.7\times$ and $1.8\times$ the $0.474$ of the $k$-core.
%
On \textsf{com-youtube} every size is far from the ground-truth groups, with F1 below $0.04$.
%
Its groups are known to be sparse~\cite{dblp}, and the comparison says nothing there.

\expsection{Case Study II: Amazon products across sizes}
% 2026-09-22 compaction: eleven sentences.
We study \textsf{com-amazon} joined with the SNAP product metadata (titles, groups and category paths), available for $334{,}852$ of its $334{,}863$ products.
%
For a query product $q$, the \textit{leaf purity} of a community is the fraction of its members whose leaf category is that of $q$.
%
Its \textit{subject purity} is the fraction whose subject, the third level of the category tree such as Jazz or Computers \& Internet, is that of $q$.
%
We follow $5{,}000$ products, drawn uniformly among those that lie in a triangle, through their own-level community at every size.
%
\sstitle{Purity rises and the communities shrink with the clique size.}
At size $2$ (the $k$-core), three quarters of the $5{,}000$ products sit in one core of $157{,}331$ products at $10$ percent leaf purity.
%
Size $3$ brings the median community to $38$ products at $44$ percent leaf purity, size $4$ to $11$ products at $70$ percent, and size $5$ to $8$ products at $79$ percent.
%
From size $4$ on, the most common subject of a community covers $99$ percent of its members on average.
%
\sstitle{The communities look like shelves.}
% 2026-09-22: the four-product table folded into the text (case/amazon-queries.json: Kind of Blue s=5 members; Introduction to Algorithms s=4 13 members; Fellowship 36,878/13,363/56 at 0.03/0.03/0.95; Godfather 28 at 0.32).
``Kind of Blue'' goes from $36{,}878$ products at size $2$, $1$ percent of them jazz, to $23$ albums of the Blue Note label at size $3$.
%
At size $5$ it is six jazz albums: Kind of Blue, The Best of the Blue Note Years, Monk's Dream, Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane, Mingus Ah Um and Saxophone Colossus.
%
``Introduction to Algorithms'' goes from the $157{,}331$-product core to $57$ computing books at size $3$ and $13$ theory textbooks at size $4$.
%
Approximation Algorithms, Randomized Algorithms and Introduction to Automata Theory are among the $13$.
%
``The Fellowship of the Ring'' still sits in $13{,}363$ products at size $3$, $3$ percent of them in its category, and reaches $56$ titles at $95$ percent leaf purity at size $4$.
%
The Godfather soundtrack reaches $28$ products at size $5$ at a leaf purity of only $32$ percent.
%
They still form one shelf, the four Godfather soundtracks among albums of Italian-American singers such as Jerry Vale and Lou Monte, a community the category tree has no name for.
%
\sstitle{Practical guideline.}
Size $3$ is the first size at which the median community, $38$ products, is small enough to read as a list.
%
Sizes $4$ and $5$ bring it to a shelf of $8$ to $11$ products at $70$ to $79$ percent leaf purity, each a few ranges listed in under $50$~ns.
